caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 173 of 1996 with Civil Rule No. 300 (FM) of 1996.
lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Rokanuddin Mahmud. Faisal Mahmud Faizee and Mobina Asaf Rahmann, Advocates — For the Appellants. 
Amirul Islam with Ms. Tania Amir, Shamsul Alam, Advocates — For Respondents.
parties:
Lawrence Loat Ltd and others  ----- Appellants
VS.
AJAX Incorporated and Siltrade International Ltd -----  Respondents.
full_judgment:
7. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the defendant appellant, have firstly given a synopsis of the palintiff's case and then started to make their submission challenging firstly, the validity of the first part of the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that the attachment of a vessel is a matter of extraordinary jurisdiction of a court which must be exercised continuously and sparingly. He submits that the plaintiffs must show that there is an attempt to remove the property or the vessel with a definite intention to defeat the decree that may be passed in favour of the plaintiff in the suit and that the show cause as may be issued by the court must be a meaningful and effective show cause clearly specifying the amount of security as per provisions of rule 5 of the Order 38 CPC. The learned Advocate said that there must be a clear prayer also in the application for attachment under Order 38 rule 5 CPC. Then the learned Advocate drew our attention to the application filed by the plaintiff under Order 38 rule 5 CPC and said that there is no definite statement in the application or in the plaint about any attempt made by the defendants to remove the vessel out of the Port Jetty. 

 10. The same statement has been made in the application under Order 38 rule 5 CPC. By a reading of the copy of the application we do not find any specific statement of any attempt made by the defendant to remove the vessel from the port except a statement made in paragraph 28 in the application to the effect "that the plaintiff is now threatened that the defendants would remove the vessel in order to avoid the claim or decree that may be passed in favour of the plaintiff." But it is not stated as to when, how and where and by whom the plaintiff was threatened that the defendants would remove the vessel. It appears that it is simply a general and a vague allegation made in the application and also in the plaint so far as the threatening is concerned. The ship arrived in the Mongla Port on 24-10-96 and duly informed the plaintiffs about its arrival and readiness to discharge the cargo and requested the plaintiff to make payment of the freight. The suit was filed on 28-10-96 only after 3 days. Then where was the time for the ship to run away from the port. The cargo was booked for the Buyer, Meghna Cement Ltd. The Buyer was to receive the goods. But he is not coming to the scene as a party to say anything in respect of ship's movement. 

 "The power which has been conferred on the court under the provision of Order XXXVIII Rule 5 CPC is an extraordinary power whereby a party in the suit may be prevented from use and enjoyment of his own properties, before any decree has at all been passed against him, and when there is no certainty that a decree will at all be passed against him. This power, must, therefore, be used with utmost caution and should be sparingly exercised. It is clear that before issuing an order under the said provisions of the Code, the court must be satisfied that the defendant has been trying to frustrate the effect of the decree that may be passed against him by disposing of his property or removing it from the jurisdiction of the court. That is to say, the court must be satisfied not only that the defendant is about to dispose of his property or remove it from its jurisdiction but also that this disposal or removal is with the object of obstructing or delaying the execution of any decree that may be passed against him. This satisfaction. however, is to be judicial satisfaction and it must be based on some materials, which are to be found in the affidavit filed by the party or otherwise. It is true that an order of attachment under this provision is to be passed on the basis of an application made by the plaintiff and an order of conditional attachment may be passed even ex parte. It is, of couse, to be borne in mind that it is difficult to produce any conclusive evidence before the court to prove the intention of a party which is secretly conceived and sought to be surreptitiously executed but even then, there must be some concrete allegations before the court about the actions of the defendant and some materials in support thereof. Otherwise, this provision of law is likely to be turned into an instrument of oppression and great harassment." 

 "The court shall have to be satisfied not only that the defendant is trying to dispose of certain property or remove certain property from the jurisdiction of the Court but also that he has been doing so with an intention to obstruct or delay the execution of the decree which may be passed against him." 

 13. It has been further observed therein that even if the apprehension of the plaintiffs is well-based such kind of difficulty is not a sufficient ground for taking recourse to the provision of Order 38 rules 5 and 6 when the said provision makes it quite clear that it should be invoked only when the removal of the certain property is sought to be made with an intent to obstruct or delay the execution of a prospective decree which may be passed against the defendants." 

 16. From the principles as laid down in the above cited decisions it appears that for the purpose of invoking the power under Order 38 rule 5 CPC for attachment before judgment there must be some concrete allegations in the application made before the court with sufficient materials of evidence to satisfy the court that the defendants have been doing an act for removing certain property or the vessel in question from the jurisdiction of the court with an intention to delay or obstruct the execution of the decree that may be passed against the defendants. In the instant case we have already stated above that the plaint or the applications under Order 38 rule 5 CPC filed before the court did not contain any concrete allegation with sufficient materials to satisfy the court that the defendants have been doing any act of removal of the vessel from court's jurisdiction with intent to obstruct or defeat the decree that may be passed in favour of the plaintiff. The statement of allegation of threat or removal of the vessel as made in para 28 of the application, in our opinion, are some 'vague' and 'general' allegations without giving any material in support thereof. 

 24. Mr. Amirul Islam futher submits that if the ship in question is allowed to leave the Mongla Port, there will be no remedy left for plaintiff to get relief of his probable decree as may be passed in favour of the plaintiff and this is again a ground for making an order of ad-interim attachment of the ship in question. But we are unable to accept this proposition of the learned Advocate in view of the following observations as made by their Lordships in the case of Messrs United Venture Navigation Co Ltd vs. Shamudrajatra Shipping Line Ltd reported in 28 DLR 231 as referred to above which runs of follows : 

 "It has been submitted that if the ship which is alleged to be belonging to the defendants is allowed to leave the port of Chittagong the plaintiffs would have no other assets to fall upon for the recovery of the money which may be decreed in their favour. We do not think that the plaintiffs will be without any remedy in respect of any transactions involving foreign companies. This kind of difficulty is likely to arise in many cases. But even then the Private international law recognises remedies which may be taken recourse to in an appropriate case in order to enforce the judgment which may be passed in the suit. But even if the apprehension of the plaintiffs is well based, such kind of difficulty, in our opinion, is not sufficient ground for taking recourse to the provision of Order 38 rules 5 and 6 when the said provision makes it quite clear that it should be invoked only when the removal of the certain property is sought to be made with an intent to obstruct or delay the execution of prospective decree which may be passed against the defendants." 

 28. By a reading of the application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 CPC filed in court by the plaintiff, it appears that the plaintiffs have prayed for a temporary injunction for restraining the defendants from removing the vessel from the jurisdiction of the court and to issue a show cause notice as to why temporary injunction should not be granted. Thus it appears that there was a prayer in the application itself for issuing show cause notice. But it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge did not look to this prayer. It has been again prayed in the same prayer portion by the plaintiffs that the defendants be directed to bring the vessel MV Gold Spring to the buyer's Jetty Meghna Cement and to discharge the entire cargo as per Bill of Lading dated 14-9-96. These three kinds of prayer at a time in an application for temporary injunction are not the contemplation of Order 39 rules 1 and 2 CPC. From the portion of the plaint, it appears that the plaintiff has prayed for a decree for recovery of possession of cargo 8800 metric tons of cement clinker and for realisation of US Dollar as mentioned therein. So, the impugned order as passed by the learned Subordinate Judge directing the defendants to discharge the entire cargo in the name of the plaintiff is in effect a decree for recovery of possession of the whole charge 8800 metric tons of cement clinker. Thus it appears that this order has given full relief to the plaintiff before trial of the suit without evidence to see as to who was owner of the goods.
